name: The Legal Ground
title: The Legal Ground
answer: Schools have long-standing legal duties to English learners under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, the Supreme Court's decision in Lau v. Nichols, and the Castañeda v. Pickard standard, all of which require schools to help students overcome language barriers. In August 2025 the Department of Education rescinded its 2015 guidance letter on meeting those duties, but that rescission changed the guidance rather than the law. The underlying statutes and court decisions remain in place, so schools still owe English learners meaningful access to grade level content.

sections.body: This idea is the legal ground beneath English learner education, the set of statutes, court decisions and federal requirements that oblige schools to help students overcome language barriers and reach grade level content. The problem it solves is confusion after a change in federal guidance, because a rescinded letter can look like a removed obligation when the obligation itself has not moved. The 2015 letter from the Departments of Education and Justice explained how schools could meet those duties, and its withdrawal in August 2025 removed that explanation, not the duties. Every Student Succeeds Act requirements for English learners still apply, and many states have their own laws on English learner education. The practical question for a school is therefore not whether the duty exists but how to meet it using the guidance that is currently in force.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not set this out by grade band, so the practice it describes applies across a school rather than to particular year groups. Schools continue to owe English learners meaningful access to grade level content, which is the standard the statutes and court decisions describe. Districts should watch their state education agency for guidance, since states may have their own English learner laws alongside the federal requirements. Before relying on any federal resource, leaders should check the current status of these changes, because the federal office that oversees English learner programs is itself in flux. In April 2026 the Department of Education notified Congress that it planned to dissolve its Office of English Language Acquisition, and advocates note that schools' federal duties remain with or without that office.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no research evidence label and cites no studies, so this idea rests on law, policy and reporting rather than on research findings. Its sources are given as Education Week (2025) for the August 2025 rescission and the point that the letter was not legally binding, Colorín Colorado (2025) for the continuing Every Student Succeeds Act requirements and state laws, and Education Week (2026) for the April 2026 notification to Congress about dissolving the Office of English Language Acquisition. The named legal foundations are Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, the Supreme Court's decision in Lau v. Nichols, and the Castañeda v. Pickard standard, together with the 2015 letter from the Departments of Education and Justice. No figures beyond those dates and names appear in the text.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text is clear that the rescission changed guidance and not law, and that the 2015 letter was never legally binding, so the limits here concern what a school can safely rely on rather than whether a duty exists. The risk is that a school treats a withdrawn letter or a dissolving federal office as the end of its obligations, when the statutes and court decisions described remain in place. The decisions that stay with people are local ones: district and school leaders must watch their state education agency, check the status of these changes, and decide what to rely on before using any federal resource. Advocates quoted in the text make the same point, that federal duties to these students remain with or without the office. This page describes practice and the text's account of the law, and it is not legal advice.
